local-seo|dentists: Most people looking for a dentist in San Antonio start in the Map Pack. They type 'dentist near me,' look at the three results, and pick based on distance, star rating, and how many reviews show up. Your office location is already set, so the real game is the rating and the review count. The other thing that trips up most dental practices here is the insurance keyword question. Yes, you can rank for 'Delta Dental dentist in Stone Oak,' but those searches act more like a directory lookup than a buying decision. The bigger lever is treating your Google Business Profile like the front page of the practice. Fresh photos, accurate hours, the right service categories, and a steady drip of reviews instead of one big push.
local-seo|hvac: HVAC works completely differently from dental. It's panic-driven. Somebody's AC quits at 2 PM in July, they grab their phone, type 'AC repair near me' or 'AC repair Stone Oak,' and call whoever shows up first and answers. The window between search and call is maybe twenty minutes. So Local SEO for HVAC isn't really about building a reputation slowly. It's about showing up in the three-pack at the exact moment someone needs you. That means citation density, a fully-built-out Google Business Profile, and service area pages on your site that match the way people actually search. Most agencies skip the citation work because it's tedious. That's also why most HVAC sites don't rank.
local-seo|restaurants: Restaurants are weird because there are really two different searches happening, and you need to win both. 'Tacos near me' is the Map Pack game (proximity, photos, reviews). 'Best tacos in San Antonio' is a different beast entirely, and usually a Yelp page or some 'best of' list outranks the restaurant's own website. So Local SEO for a restaurant means playing both sides. The Google Business Profile needs to be loaded with current photos and a steady stream of reviews, and the actual website needs to be doing the structured-data work to compete for the reputation searches. The thing most restaurant owners underestimate is how much photos matter. For restaurants, photos are a ranking factor in a way they just aren't for other businesses.
website-design|dentists: A dental practice website really only has one job: get the right person to fill out the new-patient form. Everything else on the page either helps that or gets in the way. The most common mistake I see is treating the homepage like a brochure (service lists, stock photos of smiling people, mission statements) when what actually converts is the insurance-accepted page, the team photos with real names, and a form that doesn't ask for someone's life story before they can request an appointment. For cosmetic practices, the before-and-after gallery does heavy lifting that no amount of copy can replicate. HIPAA matters too, but mostly in how the form data is handled, not in the visible design.
website-design|hvac: An HVAC website has to do two completely different things on the same domain, and most fail at both. The first job is the emergency customer. AC just quit, they're on their phone, they need a giant click-to-call button above the fold and a service area map that confirms you actually cover their neighborhood. The second job is the planned-replacement customer. Different mindset, longer decision, wants to see financing options, brand affiliations, and reviews from people whose situation looks like theirs. These two journeys need different paths on the same site. Trying to design one page that serves both is why most HVAC websites read as generic. The fix is structure, not better copy.
website-design|restaurants: Most restaurant websites should be one page, not ten. The customer landing on a restaurant site wants three things in the first two seconds: hours, location, phone number. Then maybe menu, then maybe reservations. Everything else (the about page, the chef's bio, the press section) almost nobody reads. The biggest crime in restaurant web design is still the menu-as-PDF. A PDF menu is a download on mobile, which is where eighty percent of your traffic is coming from. That single decision kills more conversions than any other design choice. Reservations integration matters if you take them, but if you don't, don't pretend you do. Simple, mobile-first, fast. That's the entire brief.
ppc-google-ads|dentists: Google Ads for a dental practice should almost always be Search campaigns, not Performance Max. Pmax sounds appealing because it's automated, but it tends to burn budget on display impressions that don't drive new-patient calls. Search lets you control exactly what you're paying for: 'dentist Stone Oak,' 'emergency dentist San Antonio,' 'Invisalign cost.' The new-patient cost-per-lead in San Antonio usually lands between $50 and $150 depending on specialty, which sounds high until you remember a single new patient is worth two to five thousand dollars over time. The mistake we see most often is running broad match to 'save time.' Broad match for dental will spend your monthly budget in a week on searches you didn't mean to buy.
ppc-google-ads|hvac: For HVAC, the conversation usually starts with whether to run Local Service Ads or traditional Search, and the right answer for San Antonio is usually both, but for different reasons. LSAs put you at the top with a Google Guaranteed badge and pay-per-lead pricing, which protects you against bad clicks. Traditional Search lets you control the ad copy and landing page, which matters more than you'd think when someone's AC just quit. The other piece most agencies miss is dayparting. A 2 PM emergency search needs different ad copy than a 2 AM one. 'Open now, on the way in 30 minutes' hits differently at different hours. And if you're not call-tracking every lead by source, you're guessing at what's working.
ppc-google-ads|restaurants: Most restaurants shouldn't be running Google Ads, and I'll say that out loud even though it costs us business. The math usually doesn't work. A $15 ticket can't absorb an $8 cost-per-click. Where ads do make sense for restaurants is in two specific cases. The first is catering and private events, where one booking is worth thousands and the CPL math actually pencils. The second is brand-search defense, running ads on your own restaurant's name so DoorDash and Yelp don't intercept the customer who was specifically looking for you. Beyond those two cases, restaurant marketing budget is almost always better spent on the Google Business Profile, photos, and reviews than on paid ads.
social-media|dentists: Social media for a dental practice splits along the channel question first. Instagram works for cosmetic and ortho practices because the before-and-after is the entire pitch. Straight-on shots of veneers, Invisalign progress, smile transformations with patient consent. Facebook still works for general family practice because that's where the parents booking appointments actually live. The content cadence that converts isn't the polished campaign. It's team photos with real names, the occasional behind-the-scenes shot, and patient testimonials with permission to use first name and photo. The metric most practices chase is engagement, but engagement is vanity. What actually moves new-patient inquiries is content that builds enough familiarity that a parent already feels like they've met the team before they call.
social-media|hvac: I'll be direct: most HVAC companies waste money on social media. The customer flow is wrong for the channel. Someone whose AC just died isn't scrolling Instagram for a contractor. They're searching Google. So social media for HVAC has to serve a different purpose than for most businesses, which is mainly recruiting and long-term brand trust. Posting before-and-after install photos, equipment knowledge content, and team highlights builds enough familiarity that when a customer does need you eventually, your name is already in their head. The other place it works is local Facebook groups, where someone asks 'who do you use for AC?' and your previous customers tag you. That's where social actually generates leads for HVAC, and almost nobody manages it deliberately.
social-media|restaurants: Restaurants are the one vertical where social media is actually a primary marketing channel. Instagram is where customers decide where to eat in the next two hours. They scroll, they see a plate that looks good, they tap directions. So the photography baseline isn't optional. It's the entire game. Phone photos are fine if the lighting is right and the framing is intentional. What kills most restaurant accounts is inconsistency, posting six times in one week then nothing for a month. The cadence matters more than the production value. Reels outperform static posts right now for reach, but static posts still convert better for established neighborhood spots where regulars already know the food. TikTok matters if your concept is novel or visual. For most spots, it's a distraction from getting Instagram right.
